title: 5 Best Residency Scheduling Software Tools for GME Programs
description: Five residency scheduling options for GME programs, a managed service, the spreadsheet, QGenda, Amion and Lightning Bolt, compared on who builds the schedule.
content:
Summary

  • Manual residency scheduling with spreadsheets is labor-intensive, error-prone, and creates significant ACGME compliance risks.
  • The loss of institutional scheduling knowledge with each chief resident rotation is a major structural problem for GME programs.
  • The market offers two primary solutions: self-service software you operate yourself, and managed services that deliver a finished schedule for you.
  • Programs that hand us the build move from building the schedule to reviewing it, and a published study found that a rebuilt call schedule improved perceived fairness.
  • For programs that want to hand off the administrative burden, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard delivers finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements, with no software to learn or operate.

You inherited the spreadsheet on July 1st. By July 3rd, you'd already discovered two conflicting rotations, a resident double-booked on overnight call, and a clinic block that somehow violated ACGME duty hour limits. Welcome to being chief resident. It's a story program coordinators and chief residents across the country know by heart. As one chief put it, "Creating residency schedules in Excel is laborious and frustrating," and plenty of others say the same. You're juggling dozens of residents across numerous rotations, tracking vacation requests, moonlighting, conference days, and subspecialty-specific ACGME rules, all while trying to make sure no one feels like they got stuck with every undesirable call shift.

And the stakes aren't just administrative. A single slip, a missed duty hour limit or an untracked consecutive shift, is easy to make and hard to spot. The risk is real, and it falls squarely on whoever's holding the spreadsheet.

There's a deeper structural problem too: institutional scheduling knowledge walks out the door every June. A new chief resident inherits a broken system and has to reinvent the wheel, usually with minimal documentation and maximum pressure.

The good news is that you have more than one kind of option.

Since we review ourselves alongside the others, you should know we are Scheduling Wizard, a service that builds physician schedules. Read our entry with that in mind. The list is ordered by who builds the schedule: a service, then the spreadsheet, then software and the platforms you publish through. Pick cost or mobile app as the measure and the order changes. Other tools are described as their own users and documentation describe them.

Two Approaches to Solving the Scheduling Problem

Before reviewing the tools, consider the fundamental fork in the road:

Self-Service Platforms: you purchase a software license, go through onboarding and training, and use the platform's tools to build and manage schedules yourself. You're the operator. The software gives you structure and rules, but the cognitive load of actually building the schedule remains yours.

Managed / Done-for-You Services: you provide your program's rules (ACGME rules, rotation requirements, resident preferences, call structure), and an expert team or service builds the schedule for you. Your role becomes reviewing and approving, not building.

The right choice depends on one question: Do you want to operate scheduling software, or do you want a finished schedule built to your rules delivered to you?

With that frame in mind, here are five residency scheduling options for GME programs.

Managed / Done-for-You Scheduling Services

1. Scheduling Wizard

Best for: Residency and fellowship programs that want to hand off schedule creation, with no software to learn or rules to configure.

Scheduling Wizard is not a software platform; it's a managed scheduling service built for GME programs, provider groups and practices. You send your program's rules: rotations, call structure, clinic days, the ACGME requirements that apply, resident preferences, vacation blocks. Our team takes it from there and delivers finished Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

There is no rule-writing interface to master and no software to implement; onboarding is a conversation about your rules. The schedule is built for you.

What is different:

  • The ACGME requirements you tell us apply are built in, not just checked afterwards. The subspecialty requirements you tell us apply go in too; it is the first question programs ask, so we ask it back.
  • Institutional continuity persists across chief rotations. When your chief graduates, the scheduling knowledge doesn't leave with them. The rules live with us, not in one person's head.
  • Your platform, your choice. Upload our schedules into the platform you already use, use the live view we build, or both.
  • Fair call distribution is built in. Call distribution equity, vacation preference integration, and cross-schedule dependency resolution are handled in the build.
  • Redrafts for bigger changes. When a resident goes on leave or a rotation moves, our team rebuilds the rest of the block to the same rules rather than leaving a manual scramble.

Scheduling Wizard is YC-backed (W26) and currently serves 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments. Pricing is quoted per program. Worth weighing against what chief residents and coordinators spend in hours annually trying to build compliant schedules manually.

Who builds the schedule? We do.

schedulingwiz.com

What you get: finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules in the format your program wants, as Excel or Google Sheets, with a custom live view if you want one. Major redrafts through the year are included. For the specifics, see our page on GME scheduling.

Do It Yourself: Spreadsheets, Software and Publishing Platforms

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best for: Programs that want complete control over the rules and have someone with the hours to apply them.

Ranked ahead of the platforms because it is what many programs actually run. A spreadsheet will hold any requirement you can state, and it does not ask you to fit your program into someone else's model. Sheets handles co-chiefs in the same file and keeps a record of what changed.

The limitation is that it does none of the work. Duty hour averages, call equity and the dependencies between block, call and clinic are all yours to track. And when the chief who built it graduates, the file stays but the reasoning behind it does not.

3. QGenda

Best for: Large health systems that need enterprise-grade scheduling with deep integration across departments, payroll, and HR systems.

QGenda is a widely used physician scheduling platform. It offers powerful, customizable rule configuration for automated schedule generation, built-in ACGME compliance tracking, and solid integrations with calendars, payroll systems, and EHRs, making it a central scheduling hub for large organizations managing dozens of departments simultaneously.

The tradeoff is significant upfront investment. As one chief resident put it on Reddit: "QGenda is a TON of work upfront but then is basically set and forget after that." Implementation takes real time, and setting up your program's specific rules usually needs a trained administrator.

As with most enterprise platforms, pricing is quoted through sales.

For a smaller, single-specialty program, it may be more platform than you need. For large academic medical centers managing complex multi-department scheduling, it's a legitimate enterprise solution.

Who builds the schedule? You do.

qgenda.com

4. Amion

Best for: Programs that need a simple, familiar tool for viewing and publishing on-call schedules.

Amion is widely used in residency programs, and many residents and attendings already know it. It is a straightforward platform for publishing on-call schedules, letting residents check their assignments and making swaps easier.

The limitation: Amion is built to publish the schedule. Building it is separate work. As one resident put it, "We used Amion. Being able to swap between ourselves was fine", but the underlying schedule still has to be built somewhere else, usually in a spreadsheet or by importing from another system.

This is why many programs we work with use both: we handle the complex schedule building, then the output is uploaded to Amion for daily viewing and access. The two tools are complementary, not competitive.

Who builds the schedule? You do; Amion publishes it.

amion.com

5. Lightning Bolt

Best for: Programs that need detailed GME requirement tracking, reporting, and rule-assisted shift scheduling for large residencies.

Lightning Bolt generates schedules from configured rules and is particularly strong for complex, shift-based programs with large resident cohorts. Its GME-specific reporting features stand out, useful when you need to demonstrate compliance during program reviews or ACGME site visits.

It helps build shift patterns, and your team still sets up the rules and reviews the result. It makes the process faster and easier to audit, and the build still sits with you.

Who builds the schedule? You do.

lightningbolt.com

The Decision Matrix: Which Tool Is Right for Your Program?

The choice between these residency scheduling software options is less about feature counts than about where you want the responsibility to sit.

If you want to operate the software yourself:

  • Need enterprise-wide integration across a large health system? QGenda
  • Need rule-based shift generation and GME audit reporting? Lightning Bolt
  • Want complete control of the rules and have the hours to apply them? Excel / Google Sheets
  • Just need a simple, familiar tool for publishing call schedules? Amion

If you want someone to build the schedule for you:

Scheduling Wizard is the option on this list that does. Programs send their rules and receive finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements they tell us apply, with no software to learn.

For chief residents, this means your role shifts from schedule builder to reviewer. For program coordinators, it means the hours you spent reconciling Excel conflicts get redirected toward work that actually moves the program forward. And for programs with annual chief rotations, it means the institutional scheduling knowledge finally lives with a service, not in one person's memory.

If compliance is your first concern (and based on what programs tell us in discovery calls, it usually is), the difference between a tool that flags violations and a service that builds the rules in is not a small distinction.

The spreadsheet era of GME scheduling doesn't have to continue. The question is just which path out of it makes sense for your program.

Want to see how this would work for your program? Book a call and tell us about your schedules. We build to your rules and requests, ACGME ones included, and send back the finished schedule.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between managed scheduling services and self-service software?

A managed scheduling service builds the entire schedule for you, while self-service software is a tool you operate yourself to build the schedule. With a managed service like Scheduling Wizard, you provide your program's rules and requests, and you receive a finished schedule built to your rules. With self-service platforms, you are responsible for learning the software, building the rules, and managing the schedule creation process internally.

How does Scheduling Wizard handle the ACGME rules for my specific subspecialty?

We do not start from assumptions about your subspecialty. You tell us which requirements apply, the Common Program Requirements and anything your Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They are part of the schedule as it is built, not flagged afterwards.

Does Scheduling Wizard replace tools like Amion?

No. Amion fits alongside what we do, and you can keep it if you want to. We deliver the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Many programs keep Amion for daily viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both.

How do you keep scheduling fair for all residents?

Fairness is central to how we build. We balance the distribution of undesirable assignments like overnight calls, weekend shifts, and holiday coverage across all residents over the entire year. We also integrate individual preferences and vacation requests so the schedule is built to your rules and residents can see that it is even.

How are mid-year schedule changes handled?

That is what redrafts are for. When a leave, a resident leaving or a rotation move reshapes the block, you tell us and we rebuild the rest of it to the same rules, which spares your chief resident or coordinator a stressful manual scramble. Redrafts through the year are included.

What is the process for getting started with Scheduling Wizard?

Getting started is simple and requires no software installation or training. The process begins with a discovery call where we collect all of your program's specific rules: rotation requirements, call and clinic structures, ACGME rules, and resident requests. Our team then uses this information to build the schedule to them and deliver it to you for review and approval.

Why can't we just use an Excel template for our schedule?

While many programs start with Excel, it is a manual, error-prone, and unsustainable solution. Spreadsheets cannot dynamically check for ACGME violations, ensure fair distribution of assignments, or easily adapt to changes, leading to dozens of hours of administrative work. It adds to chief resident burnout, and the misses are hard to catch before the schedule goes out.

How much time does a managed scheduling service save?

With a managed service like Scheduling Wizard, the program's own work becomes reviewing the schedule rather than building it. How much that saves depends on the program, but the build is usually the biggest scheduling job a chief has all year. This time can be redirected from tedious administrative tasks to higher-value activities like medical education, research, and improving resident well-being.
